passage: Four Class 10 students prepared for their March boards in different ways. Vandana counted the days back from the exam date, listed each chapter by the marks it carried, and saw that Science and Maths asked for the greatest number of hours, so those took her early mornings. Arjun turned every subject into a checklist of chapters, past papers and formula sheets, and ticked things off each night. Instead of a vague sense of being behind, he could see how far he had come. Leela saw a classmate's timetable online, five in the morning to midnight, and copied all of it. It paid no attention to her own energy or her classes, so by the second week she was exhausted and dropped the whole plan. Noor lost two days to a fever and noticed that her plan had no gaps at all. She rebuilt it with a spare half-day every week, and slid the missed chapters into it rather than piling them on top of other work.

qa.q: What did Arjun tick off each night?
qa.a: He ticked off chapters, past papers and formula sheets on his checklists.

qa.q: How does Leela's timetable differ from Noor's revised one, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Leela copied a strict routine that ignored her own energy and school hours, so she burned out and abandoned it. Noor rebuilt hers with a free half-day each week, which gave her room to catch up.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling by the second week?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and probably discouraged, since the routine she copied did not fit her and she gave up.

qa.q: What could Leela do to start again?
qa.a: She could build a timetable around her own school hours and energy, and begin with a lighter load that she can keep up. A short check each week would show what to change. 🙂

grounding: Four board-exam students plan by working backward, using checklists, copying a topper's routine, and adding buffer time after missing days.
